legal.headline: Can Customs prohibit import of sex toys as obscene articles? Calcutta High Court to decide
legal.hook: Can Customs prohibit import of sex toys as obscene articles?
legal.summary: The Calcutta High Court has agreed to hear a petition challenging the Customs authority's power to prohibit the import of sex toys on the grounds that they are obscene articles. The case turns on whether Customs can use the obscenity classification under the relevant import regulations to block such goods at the border. The petition appears to contest the interpretation and application of obscenity standards to adult wellness products. The court has not yet ruled on the merits, but the admission of the petition signals that the question of Customs' authority to classify and seize sex toys as obscene material—and the constitutional or statutory limits on that power—is now live before a High Court bench. The outcome could clarify whether Customs relies on outdated or overly broad definitions of obscenity when evaluating intimate products, or whether current law genuinely permits such seizures.
legal.contextNote: This implicates Section 11 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1992 and the Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (which references 'indecent or obscene articles'), read alongside Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code (definition of obscenity). The High Court will likely reference *Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal* (2014) 13 SCC 750, which narrowed obscenity to materials appealing to prurience and lacking serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value—but that test has not been explicitly applied by Customs in import classification. Concrete points for in-house counsel: (1) If your company imports wellness or adult products, audit current Customs classifications at your port of entry—seizures may rest on pre-*Sarkar* standards. (2) Track whether the High Court applies the *Sarkar* test to import seizures or creates a separate obscenity standard for Customs; a favorable ruling could open a compliance pathway via statutory appeal or remand. (3) Watch for potential challenge to Customs' discretion without published guidelines on obscenity assessment—absence of procedure may be as vulnerable as the rule itself.

legal.headline: Prolonged pre-trial incarceration meets twin test of Section 37 NDPS Act: Manipur HC grants bail
legal.hook: The Court released the petitioner-accused on bail, observing that the case substantially rested upon the statutory presumption under Section 35, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) and such…
legal.summary: The Manipur High Court granted bail to an accused in an NDPS Act case, finding that prolonged pre-trial incarceration satisfied the twin test mandated by Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. The Court noted that the prosecution's case rested substantially on the statutory presumption under Section 35 NDPS Act—which presumes possession of a commercial quantity as evidence of trafficking unless rebutted. The judgment clarifies that even in commercial quantity cases, the Section 37 twin test (examining grounds for detention and likelihood of flight/evidence tampering) remains a binding constitutional checkpoint that cannot be bypassed by invoking statutory presumptions alone. The bail was granted, indicating the Court found insufficient nexus between the presumption and the risk factors that would justify continued detention.
legal.contextNote: Section 37 NDPS Act imposes a mandatory dual inquiry: (1) whether the prosecution has made out a prima facie case, and (2) whether there exist reasonable grounds to believe the accused may abscond or tamper with evidence. This Manipur HC order rejects a prosecutorial shortcut—that Section 35's presumption (possession of commercial quantity = trafficking intent) can substitute for actual factual demonstration under the Section 37 test. The ruling has teeth: it signals that courts cannot mechanically detain accused persons in commercial NDPS cases simply because statutory presumptions exist. *Implications:* (1) ED and narcotics enforcement agencies must strengthen factual investigation (witness credibility, source tracking, financial links) rather than rely on quantity-based presumptions to oppose bail; (2) defense counsel in NDPS matters should isolate the Section 35 presumption from Section 37's gate-keeping function—two separate inquiries; (3) watch whether other High Courts adopt or resist this stricter reading in the next 12–18 months, especially in high-profile trafficking prosecutions involving commercial quantities.

legal.headline: Can candidates with prior open/distance mode degrees enrol as advocates after regular mode LLB? Supreme Court allows provisional enrolment
legal.hook: The question before the Court was whether candidates who had obtained their preceding degrees through open or correspondence mode but subsequently completed a 3-year regular LLB from recognised universities, could be…
legal.summary: The Supreme Court has granted provisional enrolment as advocates to candidates who obtained their preceding degrees (Bachelor's degrees) through open or distance mode but completed a subsequent 3-year regular LLB from recognised universities. The Court permitted this provisional enrolment pending final adjudication on the interpretation of Rule 5 of the Rules of Legal Education, 2008, which historically barred such candidates from advocate enrolment. The ruling effectively suspends enforcement of Rule 5's eligibility requirement while the substantive challenge to the rule itself proceeds through litigation. Candidates falling into this category can now register with Bar Councils and practise as advocates during the pendency of the final judgment, rather than remain blocked at the enrolment stage. The decision addresses a gap affecting distance-mode degree holders who upgraded to regular LLB qualification but faced advocacy denial despite meeting the LLB curriculum requirement.
legal.contextNote: The case turns on Rule 5, Rules of Legal Education, 2008, which ties advocate eligibility to the mode of preceding degrees, not just the LLB itself. The Supreme Court's provisional enrolment order is a stay of Rule 5's enforcement under Article 142 (inherent powers) pending substantive relief. This is narrower than striking down Rule 5 entirely—the rule remains formally valid but unenforced. (1) Bar Councils must now process enrolment applications from distance-mode Bachelor's + regular LLB candidates without rejection under Rule 5; counsel advising such candidates should file fresh enrolment petitions immediately and cite this order. (2) The substantive challenge to Rule 5 (likely alleging arbitrary classification, violation of Article 14 equal protection) remains live in the Supreme Court; watch for a final judgment that may strike down or reshape the rule entirely. (3) Distance-mode LLB graduates without a regular Bachelor's still appear blocked and should track whether the Court extends this relief further.

The Asian nations are motivated by the need for faster transit times and reduced vulnerability to chokepoints like the Strait of Malacca, which have historically posed risks to shipping.
